title: What this means for energy traders — Wednesday, November 11, 2026

sections.overall: Today's flow is dominated by the Iran conflict and its effects on supply routes. Easing rhetoric from Washington pulled Brent below $90, and Saudi output is reported back near prewar levels. Yet an attack on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline and continued Hormuz disruption show the risk has not gone away. Meanwhile, companies keep signing long-term LNG deals with Asian buyers. None of this was verified independently; headlines and summaries are the basis here.
sections.CRUDE_OIL: Brent fell below $90 for the first time since August after Trump said the war is "effectively over" (The Guardian). Saudi production is reported near prewar levels (FT), while the East-West pipeline was struck (FT). Markets usually weigh restored supply against infrastructure risk, and a headline-driven tape is common when both appear together. A Rapidan Energy view from last week still flagged renewed tension as a risk. What's unclear is how durable the diplomatic signals are.
sections.NATURAL_GAS: EIA raised its end-November storage forecast by about 70 billion cubic feet after a warm start to the month (EIA). Higher inventories are usually read as a softer balance for US gas. Elsewhere, Hormuz LNG traffic hit an October high, but Orlen terminated a QatarEnergy contract citing force majeure (LNG Prime). Supply is recovering unevenly, and buyers are diversifying toward other sellers.
sections.REFINED_PRODUCTS: Retail fuel is easing in the US, with gasoline below $4 per gallon for the first time since August (Rigzone). Distillates look tighter: UK diesel is near £2 a litre despite lower crude, Russia is rationing petrol after refinery strikes, and US heating bills are projected up 7% (The Guardian). Product cracks often diverge from crude when refinery outages dominate, and that appears to be the case now.
sections.CARBON_CREDITS: COP31 produced a run of Article 6 items: an Indonesia–Norway purchase agreement, a Chile recognition of Verra's program, and Canada's coming CDR procurement instruments. Carbon Pulse also reports EUAs rose for a third session, with a surprise COT showing funds built length. Corporate removal buying added no new company stories today. Whether policy announcements translate into purchase volume is still unclear.
